newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yen reeling but not yet down for the count.
newsitem.headline: Yen reeling but not yet down for the count.

text.p: Although the yen was king of the foreign exchange market a mere two years ago, recent batterings from a rampaging dollar have left it reeling -- not only against the greenback, but also an array of currencies it formerly left in the dust.
But even though the yen may be feeble, it is still far too early to count it out, dealers and economists say.

"(The yen) has definitely been low within the last few weeks, but to call it a 'sick currency' is a bit of an exaggeration. Obviously, the current weakness of the Japanese economy is manifesting (itself) in the currency," said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston in Tokyo.
"Ironically, though the economy is in trouble now, it was in just as bad a situation two years ago and the yen was at a historical high," she added.
In April 1995, the yen soared to 79.75 yen to the dollar, its highest level ever. By Wednesday, when it hit a fresh four-year low of 122.86 yen, it had retreated by a bit more than 50 percent.

The yen has also lost ground against the mark, the Swiss franc, the Australian dollar and sterling. It hit a four-and-a-half-year low near 94.70 yen against the Australian dollar on January 30 and was edging close to a 52-month low of 200 yen against the pound on Wednesday.

While moves in such "cross" trades are dominated to a certain extent by the path of the yen against the greenback, with large yen losses there pushing it lower against other currencies as well, important fundamental factors continue to undermine the Japanese currency across the board, dealers said.

"For a stronger yen, you need to take care of the macroeconomic problems like banks' bad loans, and deregulation, which is needed at a very quick tempo. If this took place, you would see a fast shift to Japanese assets," said Masaki Kamitani, sales manager at National Australia Bank in Tokyo.

But one of the biggest problems is Japan's rock-bottom interest rates, with the official discount rate stuck at a historically low 0.5 percent for more than a year. This sends funds from both overseas and domestic investors flowing to higher-yielding investments overseas, a trend exaggerated in the first weeks of this year by sharply lower Japanese stocks.

This interest rate differential can make even exotic currencies such as the Indonesian rupiah and Malaysian ringgit look better than the yen under certain circumstances, said an Asian currencies manager at one of Japan's largest city banks.
"Due to high interest rates, the rupiah is starting to gain on the dollar, and so it's becoming a bit stronger against the yen as well," he added.
Despite these and other woes, most dealers said the problem at this point was less a weak yen than a too-strong dollar.

"Actually the yen itself is fairly stable, particularly when measured against precious metals such as gold. It is only weak in relative terms," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"The big question is dollar policy in Washington. If (U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin indicated any change in the point of view, you'd see the yen take off very quickly," he added. The United States still says a strong dollar is in its interests.

A turning point for the yen may come later this week at the the meeting of officials from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations in Berlin. Markets are eager to see if statements emerge calling for more stable currency rates.

Although nobody wishes to return to the days when the yen, rather than the dollar, rode roughshod over other currencies, some Japanese bank dealers said they were a bit sorry to see their currency in its present weakened state.
"Personally, I don't think a strong yen is such a bad thing for Japan. It's proof of being a strong country. Nothing comes to a country where the currency's weak," one lamented.
